content.text:
**The first artificial satellite** was **Sputnik 1**, launched by the Soviet Union on **October 4, 1957**.

When you say **“the latest satellite,”** that changes almost daily because many satellites are launched every week. As of **June 8, 2026**, one very recent satellite launch was SpaceX’s **Starlink Group 17-43** mission on **June 7, 2026**, carrying U.S. military classified payloads based on SpaceX’s Starshield/Starlink-derived satellite bus. ([new.nextspaceflight.com](https://new.nextspaceflight.com/launches/details/8264/?utm_source=openai))

| Feature | First satellite: **Sputnik 1** | Recent/modern satellite example: **Starlink/Starshield-type satellite** |
|---|---:|---:|
| Launch date | **Oct. 4, 1957** | **June 7, 2026** example |
| Country/company | Soviet Union | SpaceX / U.S. military customers |
| Main purpose | Prove satellite launch was possible; radio beeps | Communications, internet, military/secure services |
| Size/mass | About **83.6 kg** | Typically hundreds of kg, depending on model |
| Technology | Simple radio transmitter, batteries | Solar power, advanced antennas, computers, propulsion, encryption |
| Lifespan | ~3 months in orbit | Often several years |
| Orbit | Low Earth orbit | Low Earth orbit |
| Capability | Sent basic radio signals | Data networking, maneuvering, collision avoidance, precise control |

**In simple terms:** Sputnik 1 was like a **beeping metal ball** that proved humans could put something in orbit. Modern satellites are more like **mini space robots/computers** that can communicate, navigate, adjust their orbit, and provide services such as internet, Earth imaging, weather tracking, GPS-like navigation, or military communications.
